title: Graded validation and idempotent tool-gateway: acceptance criteria for structured outputs, streaming checkpoints, and tool-call resiliency
creator: Ava Chen
description: Goal: Define pragmatic, testable acceptance criteria and rollout controls for structured output and tool/function calling that prioritize robustness across streamed and non-streamed responses. This ticket covers three correlated areas: (1) graded validation levels for emitted structured data (lenient -> strict), (2) a lightweight contract lifecycle and semantic versioning for response schemas, and (3) an idempotent tool-gateway behavior for tool invocations (retries, dedup, partial-completion checkpoints) especially under streaming and client backpressure. Deliverables: acceptance criteria doc, end-to-end test plan, lightweight SDK validation helpers, and console indicators for schema-version mismatches and tool-call health.
acceptance_criteria: Validation tiers: The runtime must support three explicit validation levels for structured output: 'lenient' (best-effort parse, tolerate missing optional fields), 'strict' (fail on missing required fields or type mismatches), and 'annotated' (lenient parse plus field-level warnings). API surfaces: per-request header and per-model default in the model catalog.

Streaming checkpoints: Streamed responses carrying partial structured objects must include stable 'checkpoint tokens' (opaque strings) every N top-level objects (configurable, default 1) so consumers can acknowledge progress and resume from the last committed token after transient failures.

Tool-call idempotency: The platform must attach a client-visible idempotency token to every tool invocation. If a tool invocation is retried by the client or the platform, the target tool/gateway will deduplicate by token and return a consistent result status. Non-idempotent tool calls must be flagged in the call metadata and require explicit operator approval to be routed through retry paths.

Contract versioning and fallback: Model response schemas in the model catalog must carry a semantic contract version string (MAJOR.MINOR). If the runtime observes a client-expressed supported-min-version that is greater than the model's contract MAJOR, it must fall back to a compatible model variant or return a clear error code (HTTP 409-like) and console guidance.

Partial-emission reconciliation: When a streaming response terminates early (network or runtime), the system must emit a reconciliation record that lists the last checkpoint token, last-validated object index, and a human-readable reason. The reconciliation record must be available via the console trace and the request metadata stream.

Observable signals: Console and API-level traces must expose: validation level used, contract version negotiated, checkpoint tokens emitted, tool-call idempotency token, and any dedup/rollback actions. These fields must be queryable in the Console trace view within 5 minutes of request completion.

SDK helpers and validation errors: SDKs (JS + Python) must provide a validation helper exposing structured error classes: ValidationError (schema mismatch), CheckpointLostError (missing token), ToolDuplicationError (duplicate idempotency token), and ContractMismatchError. These errors must be surfaced to callers with documentation links.

Backward/forward compatibility tests: For every model schema change with MAJOR increment, the runtime test harness must run compatibility tests that: (a) verify older clients receive a clear error or compatible fallback, and (b) verify newer clients receive newer fields without silent truncation. Test results must be recorded in the model catalog entry.

Performance guardrails: Enabling 'strict' validation must not increase median request latency by more than 15ms at p50 on a representative throughput test (configured at the model catalog). If it does, the runtime should expose a mitigation path (sampling, async validation with warning) until kernel optimizations are deployed.

Security gating: If a tool-call would attempt to access a restricted resource (per customer RBAC/KMS policy), the gateway must block the invocation and return a structured error with reason and policy id. This behavior must pass the security review checklist before GA.

Rollout criteria: Feature gated behind a phased rollout: internal-only -> opt-in customers -> default on. Each phase advances only after passing a minimum of 25 customers on opt-in with no severe (>P0) incidents for 14 days and <=1% increase in customer error surface related to tool-calls or schema validation.
Docs and customer-facing messaging: The Console must show a short guidance card when a contract-version mismatch occurs with actionable steps (pin model, change validation level, contact support).
Monitoring & alerts: Generate an alert when deduplication rate for tool calls exceeds 0.5% for a single customer for more than 10 minutes (possible SDK bug or replay attack).
test_plan: Unit tests for SDK validation helpers covering lenient/strict/annotated behavior and error class assertions.
Integration test: Simulate streaming response with intermittent network drop; verify checkpoint tokens emitted and resume behavior using token to request missing range.
E2E: Deploy a model variant with MAJOR schema change to a staging pool; run backward compatibility tests with pinned older clients and newer clients, verify fallback and clear error codes.
Chaos test: Inject duplicate tool invocations at the gateway and assert dedup behavior and idempotency token usage; check that logged events include tokens and dedup decisions.
Performance test: Benchmark strict vs lenient validation across 10k requests at target concurrency; assert latency degradation within guardrails.
Security test: Attempt a blocked tool-call (RBAC) and validate structured error includes policy id and audit log entry.
Observability test: Create traces and assert all required metadata fields appear in Console within 5 minutes of completion.
Customer regression test: Run the opt-in cohort for 14 days and collect incidents; ticket only advances if criteria met.
rollout_plan: Phase 0: Internal canary — enable for internal infra teams only (1 week). Collect telemetry and refine messaging.
Phase 1: Opt-in customers (10 customers target) with monitoring dashboards shared. Hold for 14 days and collect feedback.
Phase 2: Broader opt-in (25+ customers) and enable SDK helpers in beta releases.
Phase 3: Default on for newly created models; migrate catalog entries with clear migration notes and dual-run options for heavy customers.
Rollback: Toggle validation default to 'lenient' and disable streaming checkpoints per-customer if critical issues observed.
observability_requirements: Trace fields: validation_level, contract_version_requested, contract_version_served, last_checkpoint_token, tool_idempotency_token, tool_dedup_action, validation_warnings_count.
Metric exports: checkpoint_emitted_count, checkpoint_resume_count, tool_dedup_rate (per-customer), schema_mismatch_rate, validation_error_rate.
Console widgets: per-model contract-compatibility heatmap and a live table of active streaming sessions with last checkpoint and age.
Retention: Reconciliation records and trace metadata stored for 90 days for enterprise customers (configurable).
risks_and_open_questions: How do we ensure opaque checkpoint tokens cannot be forged or replayed across customers? (proposal: include customer-scoped HMAC with short TTL).
Edge case: Large batched streaming where checkpoint tokens increase message size—what is the economic cost on tokens per second at peak throughput?
Compatibility complexity: do we allow client-side schemas to declare best-effort transforms (e.g., string -> int) or must runtime enforce strict typing?
Operational complexity: who owns migration support for customers with many pinned models—product, solutions engineering, or success?
Tool gateway load: deduplication state requires storage; acceptable latency impact and storage TTL needs design.
stakeholders: Engineering: Mateo Alvarez (assignee), Priya Nair (runtime lead), Daniel Park (gateway)
notes: This ticket intentionally prioritizes observable, incremental rollout and operator controls over a single 'perfect' contract design. Aim for small, testable primitives (validation tiers, checkpoint token, idempotency token) that can be iterated independently.
